stages.title: Introduction to philosophy
stages.hook: Is a ship still the same ship if you replace its planks one by one until none of the old planks are left? Make a guess and give a reason.
explain: Philosophy comes from two Greek words meaning "love of wisdom". Philosophers ask big questions that cannot be answered just by looking or measuring: What is a good life? What is real? How do we know things? What do we owe each other?

Philosophy is not only from Greece. Thinkers in Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Europe and the Americas have all asked deep questions and given reasons for their answers. Philosophy is a way of thinking that people everywhere have shared.

Philosophers do not just give opinions. They give reasons, listen to objections, and improve their ideas. Science often tests ideas with experiments; philosophy often tests them with careful arguments and examples.

example.q: A friend says: "Philosophy is just guessing." How could you reply?
steps: Philosophers give reasons, not only guesses.
They check ideas by looking for problems and answering them.
So philosophy is careful thinking about big questions.
example.a: It is careful reasoning, not random guessing.

analogies.home: At home, families sometimes argue about what is fair. Giving reasons for what is fair is philosophy in action.
analogies.city: A town debates whether a park or a car park is better. People give reasons and answer each other.
analogies.nature: Looking at a river, someone asks: is it the same river tomorrow when the water has changed? That is a philosophical puzzle.

stages.mnemonic: Philosophy = Why? + Because. Ask a big question, then back your answer with a reason.
terms: Careful thinking, using reasons, about big questions.
Reasons given to support a conclusion.
A reason to doubt or disagree with an idea.
Good understanding of how to think and live well.

misc.wrong: Philosophy is just opinion, so no idea is better than any other.
misc.right: Philosophy uses reasons. Some arguments are stronger than others even when people still disagree about the final answer.

stages.limits: The word philosophy is Greek, but people say there are philosophical traditions in many cultures, and scholars discuss how closely they can be compared.

trip.prompt: Look at the list of branches (such as ethics and logic) and choose one to read about.

questions.q: What does the word "philosophy" mean in its Greek origin?
o: Love of wisdom
Study of stars
Art of speaking
Rules for kings
questions.why: It comes from philo (love) and sophia (wisdom).

questions.q: Which is a philosophical question?
o: What makes an action fair?
What is 12 + 9?
How tall is that tree?
What time does school start?
questions.why: Fairness cannot just be measured. It needs reasons.

questions.q: What does a philosopher do when someone disagrees?
o: Listens and answers with reasons
Repeats their view more loudly
Decides the other person is not worth hearing
Asks the group to vote without talking
questions.why: Philosophers test ideas with objections and reasons.

questions.q: Which place had philosophers asking deep questions?
o: Many places around the world
Only one city
Only a single country
Nowhere before modern times
questions.why: Philosophical traditions exist in many regions.

questions.q: Which is the best description of an argument in philosophy?
o: Reasons that support a conclusion
A heated quarrel between two people
A list of facts with no conclusion
A speech meant to make people laugh
questions.why: In philosophy an argument is reasons plus conclusion.

questions.q: Two children disagree whether a lie to save a surprise party is wrong. What is a philosophical move?
o: Give reasons and consider objections
Say that only one is allowed to talk
Vote without talking
Stop thinking
questions.why: Philosophy looks for reasons.

questions.q: Match each branch to a question it asks.
questions.why: Each branch has a focus.

questions.q: Is a philosophical idea only good if everyone agrees?
o: No, a good idea can be well supported even if debated
Yes, an idea is only good if all agree
No, good ideas are the ones nobody questions
Only if the most famous philosopher accepts it
questions.why: Debate is normal; the quality of reasons matters.

questions.q: Why is "it just feels right" not enough for a good philosophical argument? Give one reason.
questions.model: Feelings differ from person to person, so we need reasons that others can examine and test.
questions.why: Reasons can be shared and checked. A feeling alone cannot be examined in the same way.

questions.q: How is philosophy different from simply collecting facts?
o: It asks what facts mean and how we should think and act
It never needs facts, because philosophy uses only feelings and guesses
It only counts and measures things
It forbids anyone from asking questions
questions.why: Philosophy examines meanings, reasons and values.

panel.q: The ship puzzle asks if a ship with all planks replaced is the same ship. What kind of question is it?
o: A question about identity with more than one defensible answer
A question with one number as its answer that anyone can calculate
A question about wood that a carpenter can settle
A question that has no meaning at all
panel.why: Philosophers disagree because "same" can mean different things.

panel.q: Explain one way philosophy is different from science.
panel.model: Science often tests ideas with experiments and observations. Philosophy often examines concepts, values and arguments, though the two work together.
panel.why: The two overlap, but philosophy is especially about concepts, reasons and values.

panel.q: A student says: "Since philosophers disagree, philosophy teaches nothing." What is the best reply?
o: Disagreement can still teach us reasons, distinctions and better questions
They are right, because if experts disagree then nothing can be learned from them
They are right, since only one view can ever be true
They are wrong, since philosophers always end up agreeing
panel.why: Careful thinking improves even when people still disagree.

teach.model: Philosophy means love of wisdom. Philosophers ask big questions and give reasons. They listen to objections. For example, asking what makes something fair.

stages.title: Logic and arguments
stages.hook: All birds have wings. A penguin is a bird. Does the penguin have wings? How sure are you, and why?
explain: Logic is the study of good reasoning. An argument has premises (reasons) and a conclusion (the claim they support). In a valid argument, if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true.

Valid is not the same as true. "All fish can fly. A salmon is a fish. So a salmon can fly" is valid in form, but the first premise is false. An argument that is valid and has true premises is called sound.

Some bad arguments only seem good. A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning. For example, "Everyone is doing it, so it must be right" does not give a good reason. Spotting fallacies helps us think clearly and kindly.

example.q: Premise 1: All dogs are animals. Premise 2: Rex is a dog. Is "Rex is an animal" a valid conclusion?
steps: Check the pattern: all A are B, X is A.
Then X is B.
So the conclusion follows. The argument is valid, and with true premises it is sound.
example.a: Yes, it is valid and sound.

analogies.home: If every cup in the cupboard is blue and this cup came from the cupboard, it must be blue. The logic holds.
analogies.sport: If a team must win both matches to win the cup and it lost one, it cannot win the cup.
analogies.tech: A computer follows rules exactly: if the condition is true, then do the step.

stages.mnemonic: Premises are the stones; the conclusion is the arch they hold up.
terms: A statement given as a reason.
The conclusion must be true if the premises are true.
Valid with all premises actually true.
A mistake in reasoning that seems convincing.

misc.wrong: If an argument's conclusion is true, the argument must be good.
misc.right: A true conclusion can come from a bad argument. We judge the link between premises and conclusion too.

trip.prompt: Find an example of a valid argument form on the page.

questions.q: What is a premise?
o: A reason given to support a claim
The final claim that an argument reaches
A question the argument asks at the end
An example used to make people laugh
questions.why: Premises are the starting statements.

questions.q: What is the conclusion?
o: The claim the reasons support
The first reason that a speaker gives
A rule the speaker wants others to follow
An example given to illustrate a point
questions.why: It is the claim the argument reaches.

questions.q: "All cats are mammals. Tom is a cat. So Tom is a mammal." The argument is...
o: Valid
Invalid
A question
A fallacy about size
questions.why: If both premises hold, Tom must be a mammal.

questions.q: "All birds can fly. A penguin is a bird. So a penguin can fly." What is wrong?
o: The first premise is false
The pattern is invalid
The conclusion is a question
Nothing at all
questions.why: The pattern is valid, but not all birds can fly, so it is unsound.

questions.q: Which is a valid pattern?
o: All A are B; X is A; so X is B
Some A are B; X is B; so X is A
All A are B; X is B; so X is A
No A are B; X is not A; so X is B
questions.why: Only the first pattern guarantees the conclusion.

questions.q: "Everyone at school has this game, so it must be good." What kind of reasoning is this?
o: Popularity does not show goodness
Strong evidence, because many people agree
A valid proof that the game is good
A definition of what a good game is
questions.why: Many people liking something does not prove it is good.

questions.q: If an argument is valid but unsound, which is true?
o: At least one premise is false
The conclusion is always false
The pattern is wrong
It has no conclusion
questions.why: Valid with a false premise is unsound.

questions.q: Put the steps for checking an argument in order.
items: Ask if the conclusion follows if the premises are true
Ask if the premises are true
questions.why: First we identify the parts, then check the link, then check truth.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a valid argument and a true conclusion.
questions.model: A valid argument means the conclusion follows from the premises. A conclusion can be true even if the argument is bad, and a valid argument can have a false conclusion if a premise is false.
questions.why: Validity is about the link between premises and conclusion, while truth is about the facts.

questions.q: "If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is wet. So it rained." Why is this weak?
o: The ground could be wet for other reasons
It is perfectly valid, since wet ground proves rain
It has no premises, only a conclusion
Rain is never the cause of wet ground
questions.why: Someone may have used a hose. The pattern does not guarantee the conclusion.

panel.q: Can a fallacy sometimes lead to a true conclusion?
o: Yes, but the reasoning is still poor
No, a fallacy always leads to a false conclusion
Only when the argument is about maths
Only when the person arguing is an expert
panel.why: A lucky true conclusion does not repair bad reasoning.

panel.q: A friend says, "My brother is silly, so his idea must be wrong." Why is this bad reasoning?
o: It attacks the person, not the idea
It is a strong reason, since families know each other
It uses science to show the idea is wrong
It is valid, since the brother's idea is unsound
panel.why: Ideas are judged by reasons, not by who says them.

panel.q: Make a short valid argument of your own with two premises and a conclusion, and say what makes it valid.
panel.model: All frogs are amphibians. Kero is a frog. So Kero is an amphibian. It is valid because if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true.
panel.why: A valid argument has a pattern where true premises force the conclusion.

teach.model: An argument has premises and a conclusion. It is valid when the conclusion must follow if the premises are true. It is sound when it is valid and the premises are true. For example, all dogs are animals, Rex is a dog, so Rex is an animal.

stages.title: Knowledge and belief
stages.hook: You feel sure it will rain tomorrow. If it does rain, did you know it? What if you had no reason for your guess?
explain: A belief is something you take to be true. Knowledge is more than belief. Many philosophers say that to know something, it must be true, you must believe it, and you must have good reasons for it. This is often called "justified true belief".

Imagine a child believes the bell will ring at noon because a friend said so, and it does ring. The belief is true. But if the friend was only guessing, does the child know? Many people say no: a lucky guess is not knowledge.

In 1963 the philosopher Edmund Gettier gave examples where someone has a justified true belief that seems to be accidentally true. These cases made many thinkers ask whether "justified true belief" is enough. Epistemology, the study of knowledge, is still discussing it.

example.q: Aisha believes the shop is open because she saw a light on. It is open. Does she know?
steps: Is it true? Yes.
Does she believe it? Yes.
Does she have a good reason? A light is a reasonable sign.
So many would say she knows, unless the light was on by accident.
example.a: She probably knows, unless luck is involved.

analogies.home: You know the kettle is hot because you felt the steam. A guess would not count.
analogies.farm: A farmer knows the field is dry by testing the soil, not just by hoping.
analogies.tech: A computer says an answer, but we trust it more if we can see how it was checked.

stages.mnemonic: Knowing = True + Think so + Reason to show.
terms: Usually thought of as true belief with good reasons.
Facts or signs that support a belief.
The study of knowledge and how we know.

misc.wrong: If you strongly believe something, you know it.
misc.right: Strong feeling is not enough. A belief must also be true and supported by good reasons.

stages.limits: Whether justified true belief is enough for knowledge is still debated after Gettier cases, and some philosophers propose other conditions.

trip.prompt: Find the sections on justified true belief and the Gettier problem.

questions.q: Which is the best short description of knowledge in the classic view?
o: True belief with good reasons
Any belief that someone feels strongly about
A guess that happens to turn out right
Something that a lot of people say is true
questions.why: The classic view adds truth and justification to belief.

questions.q: A boy guesses a number and is right. Does he know it?
o: Not really, it was luck
Yes, always
Yes, because it was right
No, because numbers are hard
questions.why: A lucky guess is true but not supported.

questions.q: Which is a good reason to believe the stove is hot?
o: You see steam and feel warmth near it
You hope that it is, so it must be
Someone nearby shouted that it is hot
It was hot the last time you were in the kitchen
questions.why: Direct evidence supports the belief.

questions.q: What does epistemology study?
o: Knowledge and how we know
The movement of stars and planets
How plants grow in different soils
How money is saved and spent
questions.why: It is about knowledge and belief.

questions.q: Which is true about belief?
o: A belief can be false
All beliefs are true
Beliefs never change
Beliefs have no reasons
questions.why: People can believe false things.

questions.q: Why do we ask for evidence?
o: To tell lucky guesses from supported beliefs
To show that we do not trust anybody
To make the conversation last longer
To make sure that our side wins every argument we are in
questions.why: Evidence helps justify beliefs.

questions.q: Match each piece to its role in classic knowledge.
pairs: The claim matches how things are
questions.why: Each piece is needed in the classic view.

questions.q: A clock stopped 12 hours ago. You look at it, see 3 o'clock, and it happens to be 3 o'clock. Many philosophers say you do not know the time. Why?
o: Your belief is true by luck
The clock is too small to read well
Clocks are never right about the time
The clock face is made of the wrong material
questions.why: Your reason was faulty, so the truth is accidental.

questions.q: Why is a lucky guess not usually called knowledge?
questions.model: A lucky guess may be true, but there is no good reason behind it, so we say the person does not really know.
questions.why: Knowledge usually needs good reasons as well as truth.

questions.q: Does having a belief that is true always make it knowledge?
o: No, it also needs good reasons
Yes, if a belief is true it is always knowledge
Only if the person believes it very strongly
Only if an adult has said that it is true
questions.why: Truth alone does not make knowledge.

panel.q: Someone says: "I am certain, so I know." What is a good reply?
o: Certainty is a feeling, and one can be certain and wrong
You are right, certainty always means knowledge
Feelings of certainty are proof that you are correct
Never doubt a belief you are sure about
panel.why: People can feel certain and still be mistaken.

panel.q: Describe a situation where a belief is true but is not knowledge.
panel.model: A person guesses the winner of a race without any information and happens to be right. The belief is true but not supported by reasons.
panel.why: True beliefs with no good reason or with faulty reasons do not count as knowledge.

panel.q: Why do philosophers still discuss what knowledge is?
o: Clever examples challenge simple definitions
Because they enjoy arguing about words
Because no examples have ever been found
Because they forgot the old definition
panel.why: Examples such as Gettier cases push us to refine definitions.

teach.model: Belief is taking something to be true. Knowledge is usually true belief with good reasons. A lucky guess is not knowledge. For example, guessing a coin toss.

points.ask: What else is needed for knowledge?
Does it have to be true?

stages.title: Ethics and moral reasoning
stages.hook: Is it wrong to break a promise to a friend if breaking it would stop someone from being hurt? What would you want to know first?
explain: Ethics, or moral philosophy, asks how we should live and what makes actions right or wrong. It is not just rules. Ethics asks why a rule is good and what to do when rules clash.

Different ideas guide moral reasoning. Some focus on results (consequences), some on duties and rules, and some on what kind of person we become (character). People in many cultures use all three ideas in everyday life, even without these names.

Moral reasoning means thinking carefully: What are the facts? Who is affected? What reasons are on each side? What principles matter? Then we decide and can explain why. Good people sometimes still disagree after careful thought.

example.q: You find money that someone dropped. Think through it with ethics.
steps: Facts: the money belongs to someone.
Who is affected: the owner, who might need it.
Reasons: honesty, fairness, care for others.
Decision: try to return it.

analogies.home: A family decides who does which chores. They use fairness, need and promises.
analogies.city: A town sets rules to keep roads safe. Those rules protect people.
analogies.sea: Fishers agree not to take too many fish so the sea can recover.

stages.mnemonic: Facts, Folks, Reasons, Rule: four steps for thinking cool.
terms: The study of how we should live and what is right and wrong.
What happens as a result of an action.
The kind of person someone is, shown in habits.

misc.wrong: Ethics is just a list of rules from adults.
misc.right: Ethics asks for reasons behind rules and helps when rules conflict or are unclear.

stages.limits: Philosophers disagree about the foundations of ethics. Some say morality depends on consequences, duty, character, community or other things.

trip.prompt: Look at the main approaches and pick one to explain in your own words.

questions.q: What does ethics ask?
o: How should we live and act?
How far away the stars and planets are
What temperature the sun burns at
How old a tree is from its rings
questions.why: Ethics is about right and wrong and good living.

questions.q: Which idea focuses on results of actions?
o: Consequences
Duty, or the rules and promises that bind us
Style, or how an action looks to others
Weather, or the conditions around an action
questions.why: Consequences are results.

questions.q: Which idea focuses on what kind of person you become?
o: Character
Distance
Weight
Colour
questions.why: Character is habits and traits.

questions.q: You find a lost wallet. Which step in moral reasoning comes first?
o: Look at the facts
Spend the money
Hide it
Decide with no thinking
questions.why: Start with the facts.

questions.q: Why can it help to ask who is affected?
o: It makes us notice others' interests
It lets us decide more quickly
It means our own interests do not matter
It guarantees that everyone will agree
questions.why: Ethics cares for everyone affected.

questions.q: Two rules clash: telling the truth and keeping a friend's secret about a surprise party. What does ethics ask us to do?
o: Think about reasons and what matters most
Pick one rule at random and follow it
Break both rules to be safe
Stop thinking about it and let others decide
questions.why: Ethics helps when rules conflict.

questions.q: Match each approach to its main question.
pairs: What would a good person do?
questions.why: Each approach asks a different main question.

questions.q: Order a careful moral-reasoning process.
questions.why: We begin with facts and end with a reasoned decision.

questions.q: Why do we ask for reasons behind moral rules?
questions.model: Reasons let us understand why a rule is good, spot bad rules, and decide what to do when rules clash.
questions.why: A rule without reasons cannot be tested or improved.

questions.q: Can good people disagree about a moral question after careful thought?
o: Yes, it happens
No, never
Only children can
Only on holidays
questions.why: Careful reasoning does not always lead to agreement.

panel.q: A class votes to leave one child out of a game. Is it right because most voted for it?
o: Not necessarily, ethical reasons matter beyond votes
Yes, a majority vote always makes an act right
Yes, because voting is the fairest method there is
No, because a class should never vote on anything
panel.why: Fairness and care for the excluded child can outweigh a vote.

panel.q: Explain why "everyone does it" is not a complete reason that an action is right.
panel.model: Many people can do something harmful or unfair. A good ethical reason says why the action is right, not only how many do it.
panel.why: Popularity is not a moral reason.

panel.q: Which situation best shows moral reasoning rather than just following an order?
o: A student explains why sharing is fair in this case
A student shares because it is the rule on Tuesdays
A student copies a friend without asking why
A student guesses what the teacher wants
panel.why: Giving reasons shows reasoning.

teach.model: Ethics asks how we should live and what is right. We use moral reasoning: gather facts, think about who is affected, weigh reasons, decide and explain. For example, returning a lost wallet.

stages.title: Socrates and Socratic questioning
stages.hook: If a teacher kept asking "why?" after every answer you gave, would you learn more or less? Try it with: "We should be kind."
explain: Socrates (about 470 to 399 BCE) lived in Athens, Greece. He wrote no books. We know about him mainly from other writers, especially his student Plato, and also Xenophon. Because the accounts differ, scholars debate how much of the "Socrates" in Plato's dialogues is the real man.

Socrates is famous for a way of questioning. He would ask people what words like "courage", "justice" or "piety" really mean, and then test their answers with more questions. Often the conversation showed that an answer had a problem. This style is called the Socratic method.

In Plato's account, Socrates said he did not claim to be wise but wanted to examine ideas and lives. Plato has him say that an unexamined life is not worth living for a human being. Socrates was tried in Athens and sentenced to death in 399 BCE. Today people use Socratic questioning in classrooms and courts to help people think.

example.q: Someone says "Courage means never being afraid." How might a Socratic question test it?
steps: Ask: Can a person be afraid and still act bravely?
Think of a firefighter who feels fear but goes in.
Then the first answer needs improving.
example.a: The definition may be too narrow; courage may mean acting well despite fear.

analogies.home: A parent asks "What do you mean by fair?" and listens carefully. That is Socratic.
analogies.city: A judge asks a witness to explain exactly what they saw. Questions help clarify.
analogies.sport: A coach asks a player "Why did you pass there?" to help them think, not just tell them.

stages.mnemonic: Socrates: So Clear? Ask, Reply, Test, Ease Out Mistakes.
terms: Asking probing questions to test and clarify ideas.
A statement of what a word or idea means.
To look at something closely and carefully.
A conversation in which ideas are tested.

misc.right: In Plato's dialogues Socrates mostly asks questions and tests answers. He often says he is not sure.

stages.limits: Socrates left no writings, so what we know comes from others, and scholars debate which ideas belong to him and which to Plato.

trip.prompt: Find what the sources say about how Socrates asked questions.

questions.q: How do we mainly know about Socrates?
o: Through writings by others such as Plato
Through books that Socrates wrote himself
Through diaries kept by his family
Through records kept by Athens' government
questions.why: Socrates wrote nothing himself.

questions.q: Which describes the Socratic method?
o: Asking questions to test ideas
Giving long speeches to a crowd
Memorising lists of famous sayings
Voting on every question in a group
questions.why: It uses questioning.

questions.q: A friend says "A good person always wins." You ask "Can you think of a good person who lost?" What are you doing?
o: Testing the idea with a question
Insulting your friend for saying it
Agreeing so the argument can stop
Closing the talk so nothing is tested
questions.why: That is a Socratic test.

questions.q: Why might Socrates ask what "courage" means?
o: To understand the idea clearly
To tease people who had used the word
To become famous for hard questions
To win a prize for the best speech
questions.why: Clear definitions help reasoning.

questions.q: Where did Socrates live?
o: Athens in Greece
In Rome, as a Roman senator
In Cairo, near the great river
In Beijing, at the royal court
questions.why: He lived in Athens.

questions.q: Why do scholars discuss which ideas are really Socrates'?
o: Our sources are by other writers
He wrote many books that are now disputed
He lived in recent times
He left no spoken words at all
questions.why: Plato and others shaped what we read.

questions.q: Match each to its role.
pairs: Student who wrote dialogues about him
questions.why: Socrates is known through others.

questions.q: Order a Socratic exchange.
items: Ask what a key word means
questions.why: Questions help improve ideas.

questions.q: How could Socratic questions help in a disagreement between two classmates?
questions.model: Questions help each person explain what they mean, test the idea with examples, and find better reasons, instead of just shouting.
questions.why: Asking and listening clarifies ideas.

questions.q: Is it right to say Socrates always had the answers?
o: No, he often claimed to be unsure
Yes, he gave answers to every question
Yes, he wrote his answers in a book
No, he never spoke at all in public
questions.why: In the dialogues he often says he does not know.

panel.q: Why is questioning your own beliefs part of Socrates' idea of a good life?
o: It helps you live by reasons not habit
It makes you wealthy and respected
It ends all doubt about what is right
It is required by Athenian law
panel.why: Examining life means thinking about why we live as we do.

panel.q: Describe one risk and one benefit of questioning people's beliefs.
panel.model: Benefit: it can clear up confusion and improve ideas. Risk: people may feel embarrassed or angry, so it should be done respectfully.
panel.why: Socrates' questions helped some and angered others.

panel.q: A scholar says "We cannot be sure what Socrates himself thought." Why is that fair?
o: His ideas come to us through other authors
Because he wrote down everything himself
Because he probably never really lived
Because nobody in Athens wrote about him
panel.why: Different sources portray him differently.

teach.model: Socrates asked questions to test ideas, like what courage really means. He wrote nothing, so we know him through others like Plato. For example, asking if courage means not being afraid.

points.ask: How do we know about him?

stages.title: Plato and the Theory of Forms
stages.hook: You have never seen a perfect circle, yet you know what one is. Where does your idea of "perfect circle" come from?
explain: Plato (about 428 to 348 BCE) was a student of Socrates and the teacher of Aristotle. He founded a school in Athens called the Academy. Many of his writings are dialogues, conversations between characters, with Socrates often as a speaker.

Plato is famous for the Theory of Forms. In this theory, there are ideal patterns, such as Beauty, Justice and Circle, that are unchanging. The beautiful things and round things we see are imperfect copies that "share in" the Forms. We can understand a Form with reason, not just with our eyes.

Plato also discussed the soul, justice, and the best way to run a city (in his book the Republic). In a famous image, the cave, people see only shadows on a wall until one escapes and sees the real objects and the sun. Many thinkers have admired and criticised Plato; Aristotle, for example, doubted that Forms exist apart from things.

example.q: Every drawn triangle is imperfect. How can we still reason about "the triangle"?
steps: The drawing is a copy.
Reason grasps what a triangle is.
Plato said this shows we know ideal Forms.
Others say we get the idea from many examples.
example.a: Plato would say we grasp the Form; others offer other explanations.

analogies.home: A recipe is like a pattern, and every cake you bake is a copy that may not be perfect.
analogies.city: A map is a simplified pattern of a city. The real city is more complicated.
analogies.music: A tune can be played on different instruments; the tune itself is like a pattern that stays the same.

stages.mnemonic: Forms are the blueprint; things are the copies.
terms: In Plato, an unchanging ideal pattern, like Justice or Beauty.
A written conversation, the form of Plato's works.
The school Plato founded in Athens.
A story about people who mistake shadows for reality.

misc.wrong: Plato said the world we see is fake.
misc.right: Plato thought the visible world is real but changing and imperfect; the Forms are more real and stable.

stages.limits: The Theory of Forms is much debated, including by Plato himself in his dialogue Parmenides. Scholars interpret it in different ways.

trip.prompt: Find the cave image and say what the shadows stand for.

questions.q: Who was Plato's teacher?
o: Socrates
Aristotle
Confucius
Homer
questions.why: Plato studied with Socrates.

questions.q: What is a Form in Plato's theory?
o: An ideal unchanging pattern
A drawing that shows how something looks
A coin used in Athens
A school desk used in the Academy
questions.why: Forms are ideal patterns.

questions.q: In the cave story, what do the prisoners see?
o: Shadows on a wall
The sun shining at midday
Gold and jewels on the ground
Real fruit growing on the wall
questions.why: They see shadows cast by objects.

questions.q: How does Plato explain that we can reason about a perfect circle although we never see one?
o: We grasp the Form with reason
We see a perfect one drawn in the sky

Nobody could ever think about one
questions.why: The Forms are known by the mind.

questions.q: Which thinker asked whether Forms really exist apart from things?
o: Aristotle
Socrates
Zeno
Homer
questions.why: Aristotle criticised separate Forms.

questions.q: Which school did Plato found?
o: The Academy
The Lyceum
The Garden
The Stoa
questions.why: The Academy was in Athens.

questions.q: Match each item with its role.
questions.why: Plato separates Forms, examples and the mind that knows them.

questions.q: Someone says: "Plato proved Forms exist." Is that fair?
o: No, it is a debated theory
Yes, it is settled and nobody doubts it
Yes, it was proved by experiments
No, Plato wrote nothing about it
questions.why: Philosophers still debate it.

questions.q: What does the cave image suggest about people who only trust what they see?
questions.model: It suggests they might mistake appearances, like shadows, for the whole truth, and that thinking can lead to a fuller understanding.
questions.why: The cave is an image about education and the difference between appearance and understanding.

questions.q: How could someone who does not accept Forms explain our idea of a circle?
o: By drawing the idea from many examples
They would say no one can have the idea
They would say it comes from a dream
They would say it is only luck
questions.why: This is a common alternative explanation.

panel.q: Why might Plato think a just city needs wise rulers?
o: He compared rule to skill that needs knowledge
He disliked everyone in the city
He thought wisdom was easy to get
He thought the best rulers should be chosen by chance or by lot
panel.why: In the Republic he links ruling with knowledge, which many critics question.

panel.q: Give one strength and one criticism of the idea that unchanging Forms exist.
panel.model: Strength: it explains how we can have stable knowledge about things like mathematics. Criticism: it is hard to say where Forms exist or how we know them.
panel.why: Reasons on both sides are part of the debate.

panel.q: A scholar says Plato's views changed over time. What does that show?
o: Interpreting him takes care
He wrote nothing at all
He never really thought about it
His works are secret documents
panel.why: Plato's later dialogues question earlier ideas.

teach.model: Plato taught that ideal unchanging Forms, like Justice, are the patterns behind the things we see. Things are imperfect copies. For example, drawn circles are imperfect copies of the perfect circle.

points.ask: How do things relate to Forms?

stages.title: Aristotle and virtue ethics
stages.hook: Is being brave the same as having no fear? What about a person who is never afraid of anything?
explain: Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) was born in Stagira, studied in Plato's Academy, and later founded his own school, the Lyceum, in Athens. He wrote on logic, nature, politics and ethics. He believed that studying real things around us is the best way to start understanding.

In ethics Aristotle asked: what is the best life for a human being? He said the aim is eudaimonia, often translated as flourishing or living well. To flourish, we need virtues, which are good habits of character such as courage, honesty and generosity.

Aristotle said many virtues are a mean between two extremes. Courage lies between cowardice (too much fear) and recklessness (too little fear). We learn virtues by practising, like learning an instrument. The right amount depends on the person and the situation, and wisdom helps us judge it.

example.q: How much should you share your lunch?
steps: Too little is stingy.
Too much leaves you hungry and may not help.
The virtue is generosity: giving the right amount at the right time.

analogies.home: A child learns to be patient by practising waiting, little by little.
analogies.sport: A runner who pushes too little never improves; too much risks injury; the right effort is balance.
analogies.music: A musician plays notes softly or loudly; the best volume depends on the song.

stages.mnemonic: Virtue is a habit in the middle, found by practice and wise judgement.
terms: Flourishing; living well over a whole life.
The balanced point between too much and too little.
Something we do again and again until it becomes natural.

misc.wrong: Aristotle said the mean is always the average.
misc.right: The mean is not a fixed middle number. It is the right response for the person and situation, found with wisdom.

stages.limits: Interpreters disagree about how exactly Aristotle's doctrine of the mean and eudaimonia should be understood.

trip.prompt: Look at the headings on ethics and politics and find the word virtue.

questions.q: What did Aristotle say is the aim of human life?
o: Eudaimonia, or flourishing
Fame and a great reputation
Wealth only
Silence and withdrawal from life
questions.why: He called it eudaimonia.

questions.q: Courage is a mean between...
o: Cowardice and recklessness
Happiness and sadness, always avoiding both
Wealth and poverty
Speed and slowness
questions.why: It sits between too much and too little fear.

questions.q: How do we gain virtues, according to Aristotle?
o: By practice and habit
By being born with them only
By buying them
By reading only
questions.why: We become brave by acting bravely, etc.

questions.q: Which school did Aristotle found?
o: The Lyceum
The Academy
The Garden
The Porch
questions.why: The Lyceum was in Athens.

questions.q: A person gives away all their food and goes hungry for no good reason. In Aristotle's view, they...
o: Overdo generosity and miss the mean
Show perfect generosity with the right amount
Show cowardice in the face of need
Show no virtue or vice at all
questions.why: Excess, not balance.

questions.q: Why is the mean not always in the exact middle?
o: It depends on the person and situation
Because Aristotle disliked maths
Because numbers cannot be used for virtue
Because the mean is kept secret by experts
questions.why: Good judgement decides.

questions.q: Match each virtue to its extremes (too little / too much).
questions.why: Virtue lies between extremes.

questions.q: Order how a habit becomes a virtue.
questions.why: Repetition shapes character.

questions.q: Why does Aristotle say we must practise virtue rather than only learn about it?
questions.model: Like learning an instrument or sport, we become brave or kind by doing brave and kind acts repeatedly, not just by reading about them.
questions.why: Virtues are habits of action and feeling.

questions.q: Which of these is the best example of the mean?
o: A student helps a friend with homework without doing it all for them
A student does nothing to help at all
A student does their friend's homework and neglects their own
A student shouts at the friend to try harder
questions.why: Balanced helping shows judgement.

panel.q: A critic asks: "Who decides the mean?" What does Aristotle suggest?
o: A wise person using practical wisdom
A king, who rules for everyone
A coin toss, to keep it fair
A rulebook that covers every case
panel.why: He points to practical wisdom (phronesis).

panel.q: Explain how virtue ethics differs from judging an act only by its results.
panel.model: Virtue ethics asks what kind of person we become and what a good character would do, not only what results an action produces.
panel.why: The focus is character as well as outcomes.

panel.q: Is Aristotle's idea that virtue is learned by habit useful in school?
o: Yes, practising kindness and honesty builds them
No, never, since virtue cannot be taught
Only for adults who have already finished school
Only for sports and not for character
panel.why: Habit-building is a practical lesson.

teach.model: Aristotle said we should aim to flourish. We do that with virtues, good habits found between extremes. We learn them by practice. For example, courage is between fear and recklessness.

stages.title: Confucius and moral cultivation
stages.hook: How should a young person treat their elders, neighbours and a ruler? What makes someone a truly good person?
explain: Confucius (551 to 479 BCE) was a teacher and thinker in ancient China. His sayings and conversations were gathered by his students in a book called the Analects. Confucian ideas shaped education and family life in East Asia for many centuries.

Key ideas include ren (humaneness or goodwill toward others), li (proper conduct and respectful rituals), and filial piety (respect and care for parents and elders). A person who works at becoming good is called a junzi, often translated as a gentleman or exemplary person.

Confucius believed that people grow morally through learning, practice and good examples. Ideas like treating others as you would wish to be treated appear in the Analects in a form that stresses not doing to others what you would not want done to yourself. Later thinkers such as Mencius and Xunzi developed Confucianism in different ways, for example about whether human nature is basically good.

example.q: A student notices a classmate struggling. How would a Confucian approach respond?
steps: Practice ren: show goodwill and care.
Act respectfully (li), not showing off.
Give a good example for others.
example.a: Offer help with respect and kindness.

analogies.home: Children care for grandparents, thank them and learn from them.
analogies.city: Neighbours greet each other politely and help when someone is in need.
analogies.nature: A seedling grows with care; Confucians saw character as grown, not made in one day.

stages.mnemonic: Ren is heart, li is manners, learning is the road.
terms: Humaneness; goodwill and care for others.
Proper conduct, manners and respectful rituals.
An exemplary person who works at moral growth.
A book of Confucius' sayings gathered by his followers.

misc.right: Confucian ethics stresses respect, but also moral responsibility. Texts say a good minister should advise a ruler honestly.

stages.limits: Scholars interpret Confucian teachings in many ways, and later traditions differ on issues like human nature and social roles.

trip.prompt: Find the words ren and li and what they mean.

questions.q: What is the Analects?
o: A collection of sayings and conversations of Confucius

A song sung at ceremonies for rulers
A law code from ancient Rome
questions.why: It was compiled by his followers.

questions.q: What does ren mean?
o: Humaneness and goodwill

The name of a city in ancient China
questions.why: Ren is care for others.

questions.q: What is a junzi?
o: An exemplary person working at moral growth
A soldier who serves a ruler in battle and loyal duty
A tax collector in a village
A traveller who sells goods
questions.why: Often translated as gentleman or exemplary person.

questions.q: How does Confucian thinking say people become good?
o: Through learning, practice and good examples
By luck and good fortune only
By birth into a good family only
By becoming wealthy and powerful and then ruling others
questions.why: Moral cultivation takes effort.

questions.q: A child respectfully cares for a sick grandparent. Which idea does this show?
o: Filial piety
Recklessness
Cynicism
Isolation
questions.why: Filial piety is respect and care for parents and elders.

questions.q: Does Confucian ethics ask people to say nothing when a leader is wrong?
o: No, texts value honest advice
Yes, always, since loyalty means silence
Yes, since silence is the highest virtue
It never says anything about rulers
questions.why: Good ministers are expected to remonstrate.

questions.q: Match each Chinese term to its meaning.
questions.why: These are central ideas.

questions.q: Mencius and Xunzi both followed Confucius. How did they differ?
o: They disagreed about human nature
They disagreed about when to be born
They said they had never read him

questions.why: Mencius saw nature as good; Xunzi saw it as needing training.

questions.q: How is Confucian moral cultivation like learning a craft?
questions.model: Both take years of practice, learning from teachers and examples, and gradual improvement.
questions.why: Confucius stressed lifelong learning and models.

questions.q: Which action shows li?
o: Greeting an elder politely
Cutting in front of someone in line
Mocking a person who speaks slowly
Ignoring a neighbour who says hello
questions.why: Li is respectful conduct.

panel.q: A critic says Confucian duties to family may conflict with fairness to strangers. What is a fair summary?
o: This is a real debate within Confucian ethics
There is no debate, since it is all settled
Confucius never mentioned family duties
The question is a silly one to ask
panel.why: Scholars discuss how family and wider duties balance.

panel.q: Explain one way Confucian ethics and Aristotle's virtue ethics are alike.
panel.model: Both focus on developing good character through practice and by learning from good examples.
panel.why: Both are character-focused traditions, though they differ in vocabulary and context.

panel.q: Is it accurate to say Confucianism is just a list of rules?
o: No, it stresses character, relationships and judgement
Yes, it is only a list of rules
Yes, and its rules are given without any reasons or discussion
Only in large cities
panel.why: It is richer than a rule list.

teach.model: Confucius taught that people become good through learning, practice and good examples. Ren is care for others, li is proper conduct. A good person is a junzi. For example, caring for grandparents with respect.

stages.title: African communal ethical traditions
stages.hook: If a person is a person through other people, what does that say about how we should treat our neighbours?
explain: Many communities in Africa have traditions of thinking about ethics through community and relationships. One famous idea comes from Southern Africa: ubuntu. A saying in Nguni languages, "umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu", is often translated "a person is a person through other persons".

In these ideas, being a good person means caring about others, sharing, hospitality and respect. The scholar John Mbiti, writing about African religions and philosophy, is often linked with the phrase "I am because we are". Others, such as Kwame Gyekye and Kwasi Wiredu, wrote about communal values in Akan thought and about how individuals and community relate.

Communal ethics does not always mean "the group is always right". Thinkers discuss how to balance the good of the community with the rights and voice of each person. Many African societies also have proverbs, storytelling and elders' councils that teach these values.

example.q: A neighbour's roof was damaged in a storm. How does ubuntu guide you?
steps: Notice that their problem affects the whole community.
Offer help and share resources.
Others do the same, and the community becomes strong.

analogies.home: Families share meals with visitors; hospitality is part of living well.
analogies.farm: Neighbours help with planting and harvesting, then share the harvest feast.
analogies.city: Neighbours gather to repair a road or help a family in need.

stages.mnemonic: We are a basket, not a single reed: together we hold.
terms: An ethic emphasising that persons become persons through relationships with others.
A group of people connected by shared life and care.
Welcoming and caring for guests and strangers.
Giving a central place to community in ethics.

misc.wrong: Ubuntu means individuals do not matter.
misc.right: Thinkers say ubuntu values persons and sees their worth as tied to relationships. How to balance individual and group is debated.

stages.limits: Africa has many peoples and philosophies, so ubuntu is one tradition among many, and scholars discuss how far "African communitarianism" can describe them all.

trip.prompt: Find the idea of "a person through other persons" and a modern example.

Ignore the visitor and keep eating

questions.q: Which scholar is often linked with "I am because we are"?

Aristotle
Descartes
Plato

o: No, thinkers discuss balancing group and individual
Yes, the group is always right

No, because there are no groups in Africa
questions.why: It is a debated topic.

questions.q: Match each to its role.
questions.why: Community traditions teach ethics.

questions.q: How is ubuntu like Aristotle's view that humans are political, community-living animals?
o: Both see humans as living with others
They are opposites and cannot be compared
Both say people should live alone
Neither one mentions human beings

questions.q: Why might a communal ethic encourage sharing of resources?
questions.model: If a person's well-being is tied to others', then caring for and sharing with others strengthens everyone.
questions.why: Interdependence gives a reason to share.

questions.q: Order an ubuntu response to a neighbour in need.
questions.why: Care spreads.

panel.q: A critic worries that strong community values could silence a person who disagrees. What do scholars say?
o: It is a real question and many stress each person's dignity
No critic ever says that
Community values never matter at all
It is solved already, so no one needs to discuss it further
panel.why: Thinkers on ubuntu emphasise dignity and dialogue.

panel.q: Compare Ubuntu and the idea that "I decide everything alone". What is one difference?
panel.model: Ubuntu says persons are shaped by and responsible to others, while a purely individual view puts the person first on their own.
panel.why: They give different weight to relationships.

panel.q: Why is it fair to say there is no single "African philosophy"?
o: Africa has many peoples and traditions
Because Africa has no tradition of thought
Because Africa is a small place
Because all African thinkers agree
panel.why: There is great diversity.

teach.model: Ubuntu says a person becomes a person through others. It values care, sharing and hospitality. For example, neighbours rebuilding a roof together.
